54173.offence: Posted hostile, abusive, and discriminatory messages — including casual homophobic, racist, and ableist language — about members of the public and his own party, in a private WhatsApp group running from 2019 to 2025.
54173.sanction: Had already resigned before the report's publication; the Committee recommended his former member's pass be revoked.

54117.offence: Failed to declare a Labour Friends of Israel-funded visit to Israel before speaking at a related Home Affairs Committee session, and separately discussed confidential details of the ongoing investigation in a live BBC interview.
54117.sanction: The visit was resolved through the standard correction process; the media comments were found to be a separate breach of confidentiality rules, which he acknowledged.

50720.offence: Failed to register the use of a London flat, and breached the Code's paid advocacy rule.
50720.sanction: The Commissioner judged the failings too serious to resolve informally, referring the case to the full Committee rather than the standard fast-track correction process.

50709.offence: As chair of the APPG on Defence Technology, failed to carry out adequate due diligence on the group's secretariat funding — which turned out to trace back, via a UK subsidiary, to the Israeli government.
50709.sanction: Self-referred the matter once the funding was uncovered and apologised unreservedly; the APPG was later wound up.

47688.offence: A further finding, after he had already left Parliament, that his Register of Members' Financial Interests entry for an advisory role with Mere Plantations was inaccurate for the entire two years it appeared — part of the same case as his 2022 finding below.
47688.sanction: No further sanction available, as he was no longer a sitting MP; the report formally corrects the historical record.

42581.offence: Offered, in a sting by undercover journalists, to lobby ministers and table parliamentary questions for payment on behalf of gambling industry investors.
42581.sanction: 35 sitting days' suspension, upheld on appeal; resigned before a recall petition could conclude.

41434.offence: A minor, inadvertent breach of confidentiality rules during the Committee's own investigation into an earlier, separately resolved failure to declare his wife's shareholding in a childcare company.
41434.sanction: No sanction recommended — the Committee found the breach to be inadvertent.

40781.offence: Groped two men without consent at a Conservative Party conference event while intoxicated, in what the Committee called "an abuse of power."
40781.sanction: 8 weeks' suspension, upheld on appeal; resigned his seat rather than face a recall petition.

40272.offence: Failed to register a TV appearance fee on time, then registered a separate payment two days after the deadline — a second late registration within a year.
40272.sanction: Apologised; the Commissioner called it a minor but repeated lapse, and no formal sanction was imposed.

40177.offence: Wrote an unsolicited letter to the Parliamentary Commissioner attempting to influence an ongoing investigation into a fellow MP.
40177.sanction: Required to apologise to the House and the Commissioner, and to attend a briefing on his obligations under the Code.

34645.offence: Travelled by train from London to Scotland, and back, while symptomatic and awaiting a Covid-19 test result that came back positive, then attended Parliament.
34645.sanction: 30 days' suspension — long enough to trigger a recall petition, which succeeded; she lost her seat.

31469.offence: Breached the ban on paid advocacy by lobbying ministers and officials on behalf of Mere Plantations, a firm that funded a trip to Ghana and paid him as an adviser without declaring the arrangement.
31469.sanction: 5 sitting days' suspension — below the 10-day threshold that would have triggered a recall petition.

8457.offence: Acted in a threatening and intimidating manner towards parliamentary staff, then undermined the sincerity of his required apology by telling a radio station he was only apologising under threat of further sanction.

7644.offence: An "egregious case of paid advocacy" — repeatedly used his position to benefit two companies paying him as a consultant, including approaches to a food regulator and government ministers.
7644.sanction: 30 sitting days' suspension recommended; resigned before the House could vote on it, amid a wider political row over the standards process itself.

21356.offence: Offered to buy illegal drugs for two male sex workers he had arranged to meet, and failed to cooperate fully with the standards investigation into the matter.
21356.sanction: 6 months' suspension recommended; stood down as an MP before the next general election rather than serve it.

18382.offence: Late registration of financial interests on nine separate occasions over several years — including book royalties, hospitality, and newspaper column payments totalling over £52,000 — a pattern the Committee called "over-casual" rather than a single lapse.
18382.sanction: Required to apologise to the House in person, and to meet Parliament's Registrar for a briefing on his obligations.

17284.offence: Failed to declare two family holidays to Sri Lanka paid for by the Sri Lankan government, then lobbied the Prime Minister on Sri Lanka's behalf without declaring the conflict of interest.
17284.sanction: 30 days' suspension, triggering a recall petition — which fell just short of the signature threshold needed, so he kept his seat.

11611.offence: A pattern of late registrations and failing to keep register entries up to date, plus a question over payments connected to a book he co-authored.
11611.sanction: Apologised; the Registrar was asked to specifically review his registration practices again later that year.

10634.offence: Accepted payment from an undercover journalist posing as a lobbyist to ask parliamentary questions, in what the Committee called one of the most sustained breaches of registration and paid advocacy rules it had encountered.
10634.sanction: A 6-month suspension was being prepared; resigned as an MP days before it would have been handed down, triggering a by-election.
